tasks.short: Check office supply stocks and arrange replenishment within budget.

steps.what: Check cupboards and record quantities of frequently used supplies.
Check receipts and outstanding orders in the {PROCUREMENT}.
Calculate replenishment quantities and estimated costs in the {SPREADSHEET}.
Review need and approve the purchase requisition in the {PROCUREMENT}.
Check supplier terms and release the purchase order through the {PROCUREMENT}.

tasks.design: Configure stock counts, reorder rules and catalogue requisitions in the {PROCUREMENT}, including outstanding orders and budget checks. The budget holder approves the requisition, and the purchasing officer checks the prepared order before release.
tasks.previous_blocker: Cupboard quantities were disconnected from purchase records. Small, irregular purchases did not justify a separate implementation.
tasks.enabler_now: Existing purchasing configuration can handle thresholds and approvals. AI-assisted coding reduces the effort of small imports or missing connectors; no model is needed for quantities.
tasks.still_hard: Unrecorded withdrawals, shared cupboards and supplier substitutions can make the stock position wrong.
tasks.human_edge: Recognise unusual demand, challenge unnecessary purchases and choose acceptable substitutes.

ambition.what: Weekly adjustment of reorder points for high-use support supplies

tasks.altitude: The supervisor spends less time calculating orders and more time resolving shortages and checking demand changes. Existing budget and purchasing approval limits still determine decision rights.

reach.task: Record withdrawals and flag supplies needed for customer correspondence.
reach.learn: Understand consumption patterns, stock units and the operational effect of shortages.

evidence.claim: Stock thresholds, catalogue matching, arithmetic and purchasing approvals can use deterministic configuration.
Physical stock checks remain necessary where withdrawals are not recorded.

assumptions: The scope is ordinary office and customer support supplies, rather than warehouse inventory.
The {PROCUREMENT} supports catalogues, requisitions and configurable approvals.
Time shares are estimates of combined participant effort, excluding waiting time.
Access estimates cover purchasing permissions and review of any personal data recorded.
unknowns: Which stock records and purchasing features are available?
Who can approve requisitions and release orders?
Are withdrawals recorded, and who performs physical counts?
Would named withdrawal records trigger employee consultation under applicable national rules?
research_questions: Can existing stock and purchasing configuration replace the calculation workbook?
Which supplies need physical counting rather than a usage estimate?
new_work: Review low-stock exceptions and supplier substitutions.
Maintain pack sizes, reorder points and catalogue prices.
Reconcile physical counts with recorded receipts and withdrawals.
Check failed imports and approval routing.

tasks.short: Coordinate office services and changes while maintaining customer support coverage.

steps.what: Agree service needs, constraints and acceptable disruption with affected teams.
Prepare a service plan and responsibilities in the {DOCS}.
Request supplier quotations and clarify scope through the {EMAIL}.
Compare service trade-offs and approve supplier and scope.
Prepare and release the service purchase order in the {PROCUREMENT}.
Coordinate access, timing and progress through the {EMAIL}.
Inspect completion with affected teams and accept or request corrections.

tasks.design: A structured brief in the {WORKFLOW} feeds a template generator for service plans in the {DOCS}, with tasks and dependencies in the {PROJECT}. Configure quotation reminders and purchasing handoffs through the {EMAIL} and {PROCUREMENT}; people approve commitments, access arrangements and completion.
tasks.previous_blocker: Service changes are infrequent and varied. Plans, quotations and responsibilities are spread across documents and correspondence.
tasks.enabler_now: Reusable service templates and existing task workflows cover much of the coordination. Small deterministic generators and connectors are cheaper to build with AI-assisted coding.
tasks.still_hard: Relocations, security changes and asset disposal need different expertise. Suppliers and teams must negotiate disruption and access.
tasks.human_edge: Balance service continuity, staff needs and supplier commitments when a standard checklist cannot settle the trade-off.

ambition.what: Move-readiness assessment for reception and telephone coverage

tasks.altitude: The supervisor spends less time assembling plans and chasing routine updates. They can recommend disruption windows using clearer dependencies; authority over contracts, security and budgets remains with the designated roles.

reach.task: Plan visitor handling during office moves or service interruptions.
reach.learn: Map visitor routes, accessibility needs and temporary contact arrangements.

reach.task: Prepare telephone coverage during office service changes.
reach.learn: Identify call-routing dependencies, fallback contacts and acceptable outage windows.

evidence.claim: Structured intake, document templates, reminders and task dependencies can reduce coordination paperwork without a model.
Supplier selection, access decisions and physical acceptance still require accountable human judgement.

assumptions: The supervisor coordinates routine office services and refers specialist decisions to facilities or security roles.
The estimate covers a small library of service types, rather than every office change.
Time shares cover participant effort, excluding supplier lead times.
Consent and access estimates include permissions and initial employee consultation where national rules apply; formal procedures can take longer.
unknowns: Which services are delegated to the supervisor?
Which purchasing and facilities workflows already exist?
Which changes require facilities, security or employee representative approval?
Which supplier and site-access information may be shared externally?
research_questions: Which recurring service types share enough steps for one template?
Can task status and purchase order status be linked without duplicate entry?
new_work: Maintain service templates, dependencies and acceptance criteria.
Handle overdue tasks and disputed scope.
Review generated plans for local constraints.
Maintain supplier contacts and access permissions.

tasks.short: Arrange maintenance and repairs, coordinate access and confirm completion.

steps.what: Inspect the reported issue and identify urgency or need for specialist assessment.
Log the fault and equipment reference in the {HELPDESK}.
Request availability and a quotation from the responsible provider through the {EMAIL}.
Review repair cost and authorise the service order in the {PROCUREMENT}.
Book the provider by phone and agree access and service interruption.
Check operation after repair and accept completion or request further work.

tasks.design: Configure maintenance intake, equipment references, provider routing and reminders in the {HELPDESK}, with approved service orders linked from the {PROCUREMENT}. The {WORKFLOW} prepares requests and booking details using the {EMAIL} and {CALENDAR}; the supervisor handles physical assessment, commitments and acceptance.
tasks.previous_blocker: Equipment details, contracts and booking conversations were separate. Occasional repairs did not justify a dedicated implementation.
tasks.enabler_now: Existing ticket forms and routing rules cover the routine work. Small integrations can reuse equipment details and approved orders without a model.
tasks.still_hard: A physical fault may need specialist diagnosis. Providers may only accept phone bookings, and access windows can conflict with customer support coverage.
tasks.human_edge: Recognise urgency, involve qualified specialists and judge whether service has actually been restored.

ambition.what: Monthly repair-versus-replace review for equipment with recurring faults

tasks.altitude: The supervisor spends less time copying details and chasing appointments, with more time for recurring faults and disruption planning. Repair spending and replacement decisions remain subject to existing approval limits.

reach.task: Triage equipment faults and distinguish technical failures from facilities problems.
reach.learn: Understand support boundaries, useful diagnostic evidence and escalation criteria.
Understand visitor procedures and what access details a provider actually needs.

evidence.claim: Ticket configuration, provider routing, reminders and prepared requests can reduce maintenance administration.
Physical fault assessment, specialist diagnosis and acceptance limit automation of the complete task.

assumptions: The {HELPDESK} accepts facilities tickets as well as other internal requests.
The supervisor arranges repairs and does not perform specialist repair work.
Urgent faults follow an existing escalation procedure rather than waiting for a routine quotation.
Access estimates include provider permissions and review of personal or site-access information.
unknowns: Are equipment references, warranties and service contracts recorded?
Which providers support structured requests or booking links?
Which repairs need prior spending approval?
Which national rules or employee consultation requirements affect changes to site-access procedures?
research_questions: Can provider routing be determined from equipment category and service contract?
Which booking steps can existing provider channels support?
Can service acceptance update the ticket without entering the same details twice?
new_work: Maintain equipment references, provider routing and service contracts.
Handle failed requests and missed appointments.
Review recurring faults and incomplete repairs.
Check that restricted access details are removed when no longer needed.

tasks.short: Plan practical storage layouts for office supplies, records and support equipment.

steps.what: Walk the storage area and measure shelving, routes and fixed obstructions.
Compile item dimensions, weights and usage rates in the {SPREADSHEET}.
Draw layout options in drawing software in the {OTHER}.
Walk through options with users and approve a practical layout.
Publish the approved plan and storage labels in the {DOCS}.

tasks.design: A small deterministic generator on the {DATA_PLATFORM} uses verified measurements, item profiles from the {SPREADSHEET} and explicit layout rules to produce scaled options in the {DOCS}. It checks encoded clearances and capacity limits, then produces plans and labels from the version approved after a physical walkthrough.
tasks.previous_blocker: The task is infrequent, and dimensions and constraints are rarely ready for computation. A bespoke layout tool previously cost more than repeated manual drawing.
tasks.enabler_now: AI-assisted coding makes a narrow drawing and constraint-checking generator affordable. Existing drawing software should be configured first if it already supports the required rules.
tasks.still_hard: Measurements, shelf ratings and handling needs must be verified. Encoded checks cannot establish complete safety or practical usability.
tasks.human_edge: Judge reach, handling effort, accessibility and whether people can use the proposed layout comfortably.
tasks.altitude: Occasional layout projects need less redrawing and labelling. The supervisor gains more options to discuss, while approval rights remain with the facilities role; the wider working week changes little.

reach.task: Retrieve and replenish stationery and stored correspondence materials.
reach.learn: Observe retrieval frequency, item grouping and handling difficulties before choosing locations.

evidence.claim: Verified geometry and explicit placement rules can support deterministic layout options, capacity checks and label generation.
Physical validation is still needed for handling, accessibility and constraints missing from the data.

assumptions: The scope is a small office storage area rather than industrial warehouse design.
The generator uses a limited set of shelving and item types.
Physical relocation is a separate service activity.
Consent and access estimates cover drawings, site access and initial consultation where national workplace rules apply.
unknowns: Are accurate plans, item dimensions and shelf ratings available?
Does existing drawing software already provide suitable layout checks?
Who approves changes to routes, shelving and storage loads?
Which national rules and employee consultation requirements apply to the proposed physical changes?
research_questions: Can existing drawing configuration meet the need more cheaply than a custom generator?
Which constraints can be checked computationally, and which require site inspection?
Does the frequency of layout work justify maintaining a generator?
new_work: Verify measurements and item specifications before generation.
Maintain layout rules and shelving definitions.
Review options against actual handling conditions.
Keep approved plans and labels aligned with physical changes.

role.altitude: The supervisor spends less time calculating replenishment, preparing service paperwork and redrawing plans. More time goes to service continuity, physical checks and supplier exceptions; delegated spending and facilities authority determine any increase in decision rights.
reach: Connect supply availability with customer service representatives' daily work.
Coordinate reception and telephone coverage during office changes.
Use technical support triage to route equipment faults correctly.
Observe correspondence clerks' retrieval work before changing storage layouts.
skills_to_grow: Configure structured intake, approval routes and exception rules.
Read stock, purchasing and repair data critically.
Compare supplier scope, cost and service disruption.
Validate physical layouts and recognise when specialist advice is required.
Manage access and personal data under GDPR and applicable national rules.
role.ambitious_version: Provide a small office service planning function that links supply availability, recurring equipment faults and planned disruptions to customer support coverage, with clear recommendations for existing budget and facilities decision-makers.

job.title: First-Line Supervisors of Office and Administrative Support Workers
